title: On Equivalent Characterizations of the Polynomial Hierarchy in Abstract Models of Computation
abstract:
We investigate machine models similar to Turing machines that are augmented with the operations of a first-order structure ℛ, and we show that under weak conditions on ℛ, the complexity class Σ_kℛ may be characterized in four equivalent ways: (1) by polynomial-time algorithms implemented on ℛ-machines together with witness strings, (2) by the Σ_k ℛ-complete problem Σ_k SAT(ℛ), (3) by k-th existential fragment second-order metafinite logic over ℛ via descriptive complexity, and (4) via oracles. By characterizing Σ_k ℛ in these four ways, we extend previous work and embed it in one coherent framework. In addition, we derive similar results for ∃_k ℛ, the constant-free Boolean part of Σ_k ℛ, by showing that ∃_k ℛ may be characterized in four analogous ways. 
Some conditions on ℛ must be assumed in order to achieve the above quaternity because there are infinite-vocabulary structures for which NP(ℛ) = Σ₁ ℛ does not have a complete problem. Surprisingly, even in these cases, we show that NP(ℛ) does have a characterization in terms of existential second-order metafinite logic, suggesting that descriptive complexity theory is well suited to working with infinite-vocabulary structures, such as real vector spaces.

      Abstract
We investigate machine models similar to Turing machines that are augmented with the operations
of a first-order structure R, and we show that under weak conditions on R, the complexity class
Σk R may be characterized in four equivalent ways: (1) by polynomial-time algorithms implemented
on R-machines together with witness strings, (2) by the Σk R-complete problem Σk SAT(R), (3) by
kth existential fragment second-order metafinite logic over R via descriptive complexity, and (4) via
oracles. By characterizing Σk R in these four ways, we extend previous work and embed it in one
coherent framework. In addition, we derive similar results for ∃k R, the constant-free Boolean part
of Σk R, by showing that ∃k R may be characterized in four analogous ways.
    Some conditions on R must be assumed in order to achieve the above quaternity because there
are infinite-vocabulary structures for which NP(R) = Σ1 R does not have a complete problem.
Surprisingly, even in these cases, we show that NP(R) does have a characterization in terms of
existential second-order metafinite logic, suggesting that descriptive complexity theory is well suited
to working with infinite-vocabulary structures, such as real vector spaces.

 1      Introduction
Algorithms are often presented in terms of primitive operations, and the complexity of these
algorithms is often measured by counting how many times the primitive operations are
applied. Ignoring the implementation details of these primitive operations is an abstraction
that simplifies and enhances algorithm analysis. This abstraction is common in scientific
computing, wherein algorithms are presented in terms of operations on the real numbers such

       as arithmetic and trigonometric functions, the exponential function, and others [2]. It is also
       common in algebraic dynamic programming, wherein algorithms are presented in terms of
       operations that are interpreted in different semirings to solve different problems [18]. Already
       at this level of abstraction, it is infeasible to solve some algorithmic problems because they
       are complete for some higher level, Σk or Πk , of a version of the polynomial hierarchy that
       depends on these operations. We describe an example of this phenomenon in a way that

       1.1    Motivation
       The polynomial hierarchy PH contains some of the most important complexity classes in
       theoretical computer science. We may characterize the kth existential level Σk in at least
       four different ways, resulting in a quaternity:
       1. The class Σk consists of decision problems L ⊆ {0, 1}∗ for which there exists a polynomial-
          time Turing machine M and a polynomial q such that for all v ∈ {0, 1}n ,

              v ∈ L ⇐⇒ (Q1 w1 ∈ Rq(n) ) . . . (Qk wk ∈ Rq(n) )M (v, w1 , . . . , wk ) = 1,

          where the quantifiers Qi ∈ {∃, ∀} alternate, starting with Q1 = ∃. This is usually taken as
          the definition of Σk [1]. Although one may define Σk equivalently in terms of polynomial-
          time nondeterministic Turing machines, we work with the above definition of Σk because
          it generalizes in a more straightforward manner to our setting of interest.
       2. The class Σk consists of decision problems L ⊆ {0, 1}∗ that can be reduced by a polynomial-
          time Turing machine to Σk SAT ∈ Σk , where Σk SAT is the problem of deciding if a
          quantified Boolean formula, with k − 1 quantifier alternations starting with ∃, is satisfied.
          The Cook-Levin theorem establishes this characterization of Σ1 = NP, which is expressed
          by saying that SAT is NP-complete [8][31], and the Σk -completeness of Σk SAT was
          established in [43].
       3. The class Σk consists of decision problems L ⊆ {0, 1}∗ for which there is a sentence Φ of
          the kth existential fragment of second-order logic Σk SO describing L. Fagin’s theorem
          establishes this characterization of Σ1 = NP, which is expressed by saying that Σ1 SO
          captures NP [14], and the fact that Σk SO captures Σk was first established in [43].
       4. The class Σk consists of decision problems L ⊆ {0, 1}∗ for which there is a polynomial-time
          Turing machine M with access to an oracle Q ∈ Σk−1 and a polynomial q such that for
          all v ∈ {0, 1}n , v ∈ L ⇐⇒ (∃w ∈ {0, 1}q(n) ) M Q (v, w) = 1. We express this by saying
          that L ∈ NPΣk−1 . The fact that Σk = NPΣk−1 was first established in [43].

           In part motivated by the success of the theory of NP-completeness, Blum, Shub, and
       Smale initiated the study of computational complexity over the real numbers in [4]. They did
       this by investigating machines over the real numbers that have the ability to write any real
       number into memory, to evaluate infinite-precision subtraction, addition, and multiplication
       of real numbers, as well as to test the order relation between two real numbers and branch
       depending on the answer. Performing each of these operations takes one time step. In our
       terminology, this is a machine over the structure R = (R, (r : r ∈ R), −, +, ·, ≤), which we
       obtain from the ordered ring of real numbers R = (R, 0, 1, −, +, ·, ≤) by expanding it with a
       constant for each r ∈ R.
           Using machines over R, one may recreate the above quaternity for NP(R). By definition,
       NP(R) consists of real decision problems L ⊆ R∗ for which there exists a polynomial-time
       verification algorithm, using real witness strings w ∈ R∗ , implemented by an R-machine.
       One may then show that SAT(R) is NP(R)-complete under polynomial-time R-machine

reductions, where SAT(R) is the problem of deciding if a quantifier-free formula using the
operations of R is satisfiable in R. This Cook-Levin theorem over R is implied by results
in [3]. One may also show that Σ1 SO(R) captures NP(R), where Σ1 SO(R) is existential
second-order metafinite logic over R. This Fagin’s theorem over R is shown in [20]. Finally,
the oracle characterization is trivial at this base level of the hierarchy.
    More recently, Schaefer and Štefankovič observed in [39] that many Boolean decision
problems L ⊆ {0, 1}∗ in computational geometry and beyond may be reduced to the problem
∃SAT(R) = ETR of deciding if a quantifier-free formula using the operations of the ordered
ring of reals R = (R, 0, 1, −, +, ·, ≤) is satisfiable in R. Notably, such a formula may only
contain the constants 0 and 1, and its satisfiability may be decided by a Turing machine [44].
The above observation prompted the introduction of the complexity class ∃R consisting of
those problems reducible to ∃SAT(R) with a polynomial-time Turing machine. Already more
than 200 problems have been identified as ∃R-complete, attesting to the importance of the
complexity class ∃R [38].
    Using machines over R, which are just R-machines restricted to write only the constants
0 and 1 into memory, we may recreate the above quaternity for ∃R. The class ∃R consists of
Boolean decision problems L ⊆ {0, 1}∗ for which there exists a polynomial-time verification
algorithm, using real witness strings w ∈ R∗ , implemented by an R-machine. This machine
characterization of ∃R is shown in [5, 13], and it is expressed by saying that ∃R is the
constant-free Boolean part of NP(R), or ∃R = BP0 (NP(R)). By definition, ∃SAT(R) is ∃R-
complete under polynomial-time Turing machine reductions. We will show in this work that
∃SO(R) captures ∃R, where ∃SO(R) is the restriction of Σ1 SO(R) to use only the constants 0
and 1, while a similar result was recently (and independently of our work) established in [33]
by restricting Σ1 SO(R) to use only rational constants. Finally, the oracle characterization is
again trivial at this base level of the hierarchy.
    Since it is possible to recreate the above quaternity for both NP(R) and ∃R, these
complexity classes faithfully resemble Σ1 = NP. As we noted above, algorithms are often
analyzed over different domains according to different sets of primitive operations that depend
on the application area. Given the importance of NP and Σk more generally, a fundamental
question in the complexity of algorithms is the following: In which domains and with which
sets of primitive operations can we recreate the above quaternity for Σk ?
    We formalize this question with first-order structures R, which consist of a set R together
with constants c ∈ R, functions f : Rk → R, and relations P ⊆ Rk . Using register machines
over R, we refine our fundamental question as follows: Under what conditions on R is it
possible to recreate the above quaternity for both Σk R and ∃k R by characterizing them in
terms of machine models, complete problems, descriptive complexity, and oracles?

1.2    Overview of Our Contribution
In this work, we define Σk R and ∃k R in terms of register machines over R, resulting in the
polynomial and Boolean hierarchies over a structure, as depicted in Figure 1. We then identify
mild conditions on R which allow us to generalize the above quaternity by characterizing
Σk R and ∃k R in terms of complete problems, descriptive complexity, and oracles.
    Each of our results requires us to assume that R is a bipointed structure, by which we
mean that R has at least two distinct constants 0 ̸= 1. Our completeness results require
us to assume further that R is of finite type, by which we mean that R has only finitely
many functions and relations. Finally, for completeness with respect to non-Boolean decision
problems, we must assume that R has all constants, by which we mean that R has a unique
constant r for each element in its universe R.

            We begin with complete problems. It is already known from [19] that if R is a bipointed
       structure of finite type with all constants, then SAT(R) is NP(R)-complete under polynomial-
       time R-machine reductions. Furthermore, it is folklore that, under the same conditions on
       R, Σk SAT(R) is Σk R-complete under polynomial-time R-machine reductions [7, 11]. This
       folklore result is sometimes attributed to [37], which is a foundational text that is no longer
       in wide circulation, preventing us from accessing it. In Theorem 11, we offer a detailed proof
       that that if R is a bipointed structure of finite type with all constants, then Σk SAT(R) is
       Σk R-complete under polynomial-time R-machine reductions. We offer this proof not only
       for completeness, but also because analyzing this proof allows us to explain why the assumed
       conditions on R are probably necessary. Furthermore, our analysis of this proof allows us to
       derive Corollary 12, in which we show that if R is a bipointed structure of finite type, then
       ∃k SAT(R) is ∃k R-complete under polynomial-time Turing machine reductions.
            We next turn to descriptive complexity theory. In Theorem 14, we show that if R is a
       bipointed structure, then Σk SO(R) captures Σk R on metafinite structures over R. Note
       that we are not required to assume that R is of finite type, nor that R has all constants, in
       contrast to our completeness results. Since there is a structure Z of infinite type for which
       there is no NP(Z)-complete problem [16], Theorem 14 is strictly more general than any
       possible generalization of Theorem 11. This suggests that descriptive complexity theory is
       well suited for dealing with structures of infinite type, such as real vector spaces. Additionally,
       from Theorem 14 we derive Corollary 15 in which we show that if R is a bipointed structure,
       then ∃k SO(R) captures ∃k R on Boolean metafinite structures over R.
            We finally turn to oracle characterizations of these hierarchies. In Theorem 16, we
       show that if R is a bipointed structure, then Σk+1 R = NP(R)Σk R . Additionally, from

   We organize our results as follows: In Section 2 we present preliminary definitions, in
Section 3 we present our results about complete problems, in Section 4 we present our results
about descriptive complexity, and in Section 5 we present our results about oracles. In each
section, we provide proof sketches of our results, as well as a discussion of related work.
Full proofs appear in the appendix of the full version of our paper, as well as an extended
preliminaries section to make our results more accessible [28]. Each section in this appendix
may be seen as an extended version of the corresponding section in the main body of our
paper.


 2      Preliminaries
We present a selection of the preliminaries that are most important for understanding our
results. The reader who desires more formal detail or more intuition may find both of these
in the extended preliminaries of the appendix of the full version of our paper [28].

2.1     Register Machines Over a Structure
A vocabulary Voc specifies a set of constant symbols c and, for each arity k ≥ 1, a set
function symbols f and a set of relation symbols P . A (first-order) Voc-structure R specifies
an interpretation of each of these symbols in an underlying set R, which we call the universe
of R. Conflating a symbol with its interpretation, we may say that R has constants c ∈ R,
functions f : Rk → R, and relations P ⊆ Rk .
    Recall that we say R is bipointed if it has at least two constants 0 ̸= 1, that R is of finite
type if it has only finitely many functions and relations, and that R has all constants if it
has a unique constant r for each element of its universe R. Additionally, we treat equality
= as a logical relation [45], so we always assume that the equality relation is implicitly
present in every structure. This appears to be necessary for most of our results to hold
in generality, though equality can be omitted in some particular contexts, as is often done
when comparing the complexity of different syntactic fragments of the theory of R, viewed
as decision problems in ∃R and related complexity classes [39, 40].
    The symbols of a vocabulary Voc constitute the basic ingredients of a programming
language in which we may specify computations over a Voc-structure R. These computations
are carried out by a register machine over R, also called an R-machine, as depicted in

           An R-machine manipulates the contents of its registers based on its R-program P, which
       is a finite enumerated sequence of R-instructions. Importantly, there are R-instructions
       directing R-machines to evaluate each operation of the structure R in the following way:
        1. the instruction Z⌊⌈j0 ⌋⌉ := c directs a machine to store the constant c in register Z⌊⌈j0 ⌋⌉,
        2. the instruction Z⌊⌈j0 ⌋⌉ := f (Z⌊⌈j1 ⌋⌉, . . . , Z⌊⌈jk ⌋⌉) directs a machine to evaluate the function
           f (Z⌊⌈j1 ⌋⌉, . . . , Z⌊⌈jk ⌋⌉) and store the result in register Z⌊⌈j0 ⌋⌉,
        3. the instruction if P (Z⌊⌈j1 ⌋⌉, . . . , Z⌊⌈jk ⌋⌉) then goto ℓ1 else goto ℓ2 directs a machine to test
           the relation P (Z⌊⌈j1 ⌋⌉, . . . , Z⌊⌈jk ⌋⌉) and go to instruction ℓ1 or ℓ2 depending on the result.
       In addition to the above, R-instructions may also direct an R-machine to branch based on a
       test of equality between R-registers or index registers, to copy the contents of one R-register
       to another, and to increment or decrement the contents of an index register. Finally, when we
       would like to equip an R-machine with an oracle Q ⊆ R∗ , we allow R-instructions directing
       R-machines to query this oracle. A full list of R-instructions is presented in the appendix of
       the full version of our paper [28].
           In the formal definition of R-machines below, we include the structure R as a component
       of R-machines. We do this so that the R-machine knows how to interpret the symbols in its
       program, and in this sense we may view the structure R as the CPU from Figure 2, while
       the other components of R-machines correspond in the expected way to this picture.
       ▶ Definition 1 (R-Machines). A machine over R, also called an R-machine, is a tuple
       M = (P, R, NkP , RN ) specifying the following information:
        1. an R-program P,
        2. the structure R,
        3. a space of index states NkP ,
        4. a space of memory states RN .
       We say that the constants of R, other than 0 and 1, appearing in an instruction of P are the
       machine constants of M , and that M is constant free if it has no machine constants. The

       input and output space of M are R∗ = n=0 Rn .
           Our definition of R-machines is taken with minimal modification from [25, 17], and it
       is similar to the original definition of BSS machines given in [4], which closely resemble
       register machines, a precursor to random access machines introduced in [42]. Because our
       R-instructions allow only sequential access to memory by incrementing or decrementing an
       index register, we use the name register machine over R.
           A significant difference between BSS machines over a ring R and R-machines is that
       BSS machines over R may write an arbitrary element r ∈ R into memory, while R-machines
       may write an element r into memory only if r is a constant of the structure R, or if r can
       be computed from an input using the operations of R. We choose to limit R-machines in
       this way so that the power of R-machines more closely reflects the operations present in the
       structure R, including the constant operations.
           An element r ∈ R usually plays the role of an input to an R-machine. When we turn r
       into a constant, we assign it a very different role. As a constant, r may encode an infinite
       amount of information into R-programs. For example, consider the ordered ring of reals
       expanded with all constants R and suppose rhalt ∈ R encodes the characteristic function
       of the diagonal halting problem. Upon input n ∈ N encoded in binary, an R-machine with
       rhalt as a machine constant can extract the nth bit of rhalt , as described in [30], to decide if
       the nth Turing machine halts on input n, thereby deciding the diagonal halting problem.
       This means that R-machines with rhalt as a machine constant are strictly more powerful
       than Turing machines, even when we restrict these R-machines to Boolean inputs, whereas
       constant-free Boolean R-machines may be simulated by Turing machines.

    Another subtlety concerning constants arises when one regards constants as functions of
arity zero. We refrain from taking this view because it would clash with the definition of
structures of finite type, which may have infinitely many constants but only finitely many
functions. Assuming that R is of finite type is useful to us because this guarantees that
R has an effective encoding, which is an encoding the symbols in the vocabulary of R as
strings in R∗ in such a way that an R-machine can interpret that code and then evaluate the
corresponding operation. In general, we will use an effective encoding of R when we show
membership of satisfiability problems over R in complexity classes over R. Note that there
is an effective encoding for R if and only if there is a universal R-machine [24].
    Structures with infinitely many constants may still have an effective encoding because a
constant may always stand as a code for itself, whereas there are structures with infinitely
many unary functions, such as Rlin , for which there is no effective encoding. To get an
intuition for this phenomenon, consider why there can be no universal Rlin -machine. Any
Rlin -machine can have only finitely many scalar functions µr in its program, and it is not
possible to express each function in {µr : r ∈ R} in terms of a finite subset of these functions.
    There is a long history capturing computations over a first-order structure with machines
and methods similar to ours [15]. We refer the reader to the introduction of [25] for further
references into this history. There are multiple incomparable ways to generalize computation
to the real numbers [36]. Machines over R given an algebraic generalization, while computable
analysis and type two effectivity give a topological generalization [35]. The algebraic approach
provides fertile ground for complexity theory. For an introductory survey of early results in
the complexity of computation over R and other structures, see [32].

2.2    Complexity Classes

We view each subset L ⊆ R∗ = n=0 Rn as a decision problem over a structure R. Under a
suitable encoding, the main decision problems we will work with consist of satisfied sentences
of a specified grammatical form. A sentence Φ is in prenex normal form when it is a string
of quantifiers followed by a quantifier free formula φ as in Q1 x1 . . . Qn φ(x1 , . . . , xn ), where
Qi ∈ {∃, ∀}. Supposing Φ has k − 1 quantifier alternations, we say that Φ is a Σk sentence
when Q1 = ∃, and we say that Φ is a Πk sentence when Q1 = ∀.
▶ Definition 2 (Decision Problems of Satisfied Sentences). The theory of R is the set Th(R)
of sentences Φ in the vocabulary of R that are satisfied in R, and the Boolean theory of R

identify the following fragments of these theories that we refer to as the kth existential or
universal fragment of the theory or Boolean theory of R, respectively:
 1. Σk SAT(R) = {Φ : Φ is a Σk sentence and R ⊨ Φ},
 2. Πk SAT(R) = {Φ : Φ is a Πk sentence and R ⊨ Φ},
 3. ∃k SAT(R) = {Φ ∈ Σk SAT(R) : all constants in Φ are 0 or 1},
 4. ∀k SAT(R) = {Φ ∈ Πk SAT(R) : all constants in Φ are 0 or 1}.

 6    Conclusion
We have characterized the polynomial and Boolean hierarchies over a first-order structure
R in terms of machine models, complete problems, descriptive complexity, and oracles.
Additionally, we have shown that descriptive complexity is well suited to working with
algorithms over infinite vocabulary structures, such as real vector spaces. In this way, we
